steps.body:
The verdict is decided by what f′ does on **either side** of the critical point.

**f′ goes + → −** : the curve climbs then falls. A **maximum**.
**f′ goes − → +** : falls then climbs. A **minimum**.
**f′ does not change sign** : no extremum at all. A flat pause.

That is a **sign chart** — the exact machinery you built in `polynomial-rational-analysis`, pointed at f′ instead of f.
Build the sign chart of the DERIVATIVE.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x, so f′(x) = 3(x + 2)(x − 2). Set the sign of f′ on each interval.
widget.successFeedback: + − +. Read it as a story about f: it CLIMBS, then FALLS, then CLIMBS. So x = −2 (where f′ goes + → −) is a maximum, and x = 2 (where f′ goes − → +) is a minimum. The chart is the same one you have drawn a dozen times — only the function it is pointed at has changed.
widget.crossFeedback: Both roots of f′ are single, so f′ must change sign at each one. Two flips, three intervals.
widget.bounceFeedback: Neither root is repeated here, so there is no bounce — every root of this f′ is a crossing.

cml.actionGoal: Set interval signs and use root multiplicity to explain where a function crosses or only touches the axis.

predict.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x, so f′(x) = 3(x + 2)(x − 2), which is negative between −2 and 2. On that stretch the graph of f is…
predict.reveal: Falling, and that is all it says. f′ < 0 is a statement about DIRECTION, never about height: at x = −1 this curve sits at +11 and is dropping fast. A chart of f′ can tell you the curve is going down; only a chart of f can tell you where it is.

explanationVariants: f′ goes from + to − at x = −2, so f climbs into it and falls out: a maximum, of value f(−2) = 16.
The sign chart of f′ tells you the SHAPE of f. It does not tell you the height — for that you must evaluate f.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x, with f′ positive, then negative, then positive. Find the local MAXIMUM value of f.

commonErrors.feedback: That is WHERE the maximum occurs. The question asks for its VALUE: f(−2) = −8 + 24 = 16.
That is f(2), the local MINIMUM. The maximum is at x = −2, where f = 16.
That is where the minimum occurs. The maximum is at x = −2, and its value is 16.

widget.fallbackFeedback: f′ goes + → − at x = −2, so f(−2) = −8 + 24 = 16 is a local maximum.

steps.body: The bounce, and what it means now.
explanationVariants: f′ = 4x²(x − 3) has a DOUBLE root at 0, so f′ touches zero and comes back the same side — no sign change, no extremum. It is a saddle.
The multiplicity rule you learned for sign charts now has a calculus meaning: an even root of f′ is a critical point that is NOT an extremum.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x⁴ − 4x³, so f′(x) = 4x²(x − 3). Set the signs of f′ — and watch the double root.
widget.successFeedback: − − +. The double root at 0 does NOT flip the sign, so f′ is negative on both sides of it: f is falling into x = 0 and still falling out. It is a critical point and it is NOT an extremum — a saddle. Only x = 3, where f′ genuinely crosses, is a minimum. The bounce-versus-cross rule has just become a statement about peaks and valleys.
widget.crossFeedback: The root at 3 is single, so f′ must change sign there.
widget.bounceFeedback: You flipped the sign across x = 0, but that root of f′ is DOUBLE. f′ touches zero and returns to the side it came from — so f keeps falling, and there is no extremum.

cml.actionGoal: Set interval signs and use root multiplicity to explain where a function crosses or only touches the axis.

steps.body:
So the whole first-derivative test is one habit:

**Draw the sign chart of f′. Read the story of f off it.**

+ then − is a peak. − then + is a valley. No change is a saddle. You already own this machinery; it has simply been pointed at a new function.
Rising or falling, from the chart.
explanationVariants: f′ < 0 exactly on (−2, 2), so that is where f is falling.
The sign chart of f′ is a complete map of where f rises and where it falls.

widget.prompt: f′ is positive on (−∞, −2), negative on (−2, 2), positive on (2, ∞). Where is f DECREASING?

options.label: On (−2, 2) — the interval where f′ is negative.
options.feedback: Right. Decreasing is a statement about the SIGN of f′, and nothing else.

options.label: On (−∞, −2).
options.feedback: f′ is POSITIVE there, so f is climbing, not falling.

options.label: At x = −2 and x = 2.
options.feedback: At those points f′ = 0, so f is momentarily flat — neither rising nor falling. Decreasing happens on the interval BETWEEN them.

options.label: Nowhere — f′ is a parabola opening upward.
options.feedback: An upward parabola dips BELOW the axis between its roots, and that dip is exactly where f falls.

hints: Critical points at 0 and 3. Test the sign of f′ on (−∞, 0), (0, 3) and (3, ∞).
f′ is negative, negative, positive. Only one sign CHANGE.
explanationVariants: f′ = 4x²(x − 3) is − , − , + across the three intervals. Only x = 3 is a sign change, so there is exactly ONE extremum — a minimum at x = 3.
x = 0 is a critical point with no sign change: a saddle, not an extremum. Counting it would be the classic error.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x⁴ − 4x³. How many local EXTREMA does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: There are two critical points, but only ONE is an extremum. At x = 0 the derivative touches zero without changing sign — a saddle.
There is one: at x = 3, f′ crosses from negative to positive, so f falls into it and climbs out. A minimum.
f′ = 4x²(x − 3) has only two distinct roots, and only one of them is a sign change.

widget.fallbackFeedback: f′ = 4x²(x−3) goes −, −, +: only x = 3 is a sign change, so there is exactly one extremum (a minimum).

steps.body: The sign chart of f′ IS the shape of f.
takeaways: + → − is a maximum. − → + is a minimum. No sign change is a saddle, not an extremum.
An EVEN root of f′ is a critical point with no sign change — the bounce rule, now saying something about peaks.
You built this machinery in precalculus. Calculus just pointed it at f′.
steps.teaser: Next: what happens at the ends of a closed interval.

concept.body: Look at f′ just LEFT of the critical point, and just RIGHT of it. Positive then negative: the curve climbed and then fell, so it is a peak. Negative then positive: a valley. Same sign twice: nothing happened.

explanationVariants: f′ negative then positive means f fell into the point and climbed out: a minimum.
The order of the signs is the whole verdict.

widget.prompt: f′ is negative just left of c, and positive just right of it. What is at c?

options.label: A local minimum
options.feedback: Right — the curve fell in and climbed out, so c is the bottom of a valley.

options.label: A local maximum
options.feedback: That would need + then −: climbing in and falling out. Here it is the other way round.
